entries.title: EyeToy camera
entries.subtitle: Your movements become the controls
entries.summary: EyeToy brought camera-based play to PlayStation 2 in 2003.
body: EyeToy is a USB camera for PlayStation 2. Introduced in 2003, it put the player's image on the television and let specially designed games respond to movement in front of the camera. The person playing became part of the picture rather than controlling everything with a handheld pad.

EyeToy: Play built short activities around this idea. The camera needed compatible software: it was not a replacement for the controller in every PlayStation 2 game. Other titles, including games in The Sims and Tony Hawk series, added optional EyeToy features.
story_headings: A camera in the living room

entries.title: SingStar microphones
entries.subtitle: Two microphones turn a room into a stage
entries.summary: The red and blue SingStar microphones accompanied the PlayStation 2 singing series from 2004.
body: SingStar debuted on PlayStation 2 in 2004 with a pair of microphones, identified by red and blue. Players sang along with recorded songs, alone or together. The microphones supplied the voices to the game, while the television displayed lyrics and the notes to follow.

Scoring compared the singer's pitch and timing with the song's guide. The challenge was to hold and place notes, not to play an instrument with buttons. The wired pair shown here belongs to the original accessory family; later wireless microphones were a separate development. The microphones required compatible SingStar software and were not a complete karaoke system on their own.

entries.title: Guitar Hero guitar controller
entries.subtitle: A plastic guitar makes rhythm physical
entries.summary: Guitar Hero brought its guitar-shaped controller to PlayStation 2 in 2005.
body: Guitar Hero began on PlayStation 2 in 2005. Its guitar-shaped controller replaced strings with coloured fret buttons and a strum bar. Players held the indicated buttons and strummed as notes reached the target on screen. The shape made the familiar rhythm-game task feel like a small stage performance.

The controller was an input device, not a guitar that produced music independently. Compatible software supplied the songs and judged the player's timing. Later Guitar Hero releases used different controller designs and platform connections, so the family should not be treated as one universally compatible accessory.
story_headings: A controller for a particular kind of play

entries.title: Power Glove
entries.subtitle: A controller you could wear
entries.summary: Mattel brought hand tracking to the NES in 1989.
body: Mattel's Power Glove combined finger sensors, hand tracking and a keypad on the wrist. Introduced in 1989 for the NES, it offered a striking alternative to holding a controller: movements and finger bends could become game inputs.

The affordable consumer device was much simpler than the professional DataGlove that inspired it. Its futuristic appearance and publicity promised more natural play, but accuracy and usability limited that promise. It remains a memorable early experiment in wearable game control.

entries.title: NES Zapper
entries.subtitle: Taking aim at the television
entries.summary: Nintendo's light gun accompanied the North American NES in 1985.
story_headings: Duck Hunt in the living room
body: The NES Zapper made aiming at the television part of home play. Nintendo introduced the western NES accessory in 1985, and Duck Hunt became its best-known partner. Its futuristic gray shape differed from the earlier Japanese Famicom gun.

The Zapper detects light from the screen rather than firing a beam at it. Compatible games briefly change the displayed image to identify a hit. That method was designed for CRT televisions; the original accessory does not simply work on a modern flat-panel display.

entries.title: GunCon / G-Con45
entries.subtitle: Arcade aiming on PlayStation
entries.summary: Namco introduced its original PlayStation GunCon in 1997.
body: Namco's GunCon, also known as G-Con45, brought a purpose-built light gun to the original PlayStation in 1997. Time Crisis was its showcase: the player aimed directly at the television, while an additional button could handle actions such as taking cover.

The controller was made by Namco, not Sony. It needed compatible software and a CRT television, with a connection to the video signal as well as the console's controller port. Later GunCon 2 and GunCon 3 models belong to different hardware generations.

entries.title: Dance Dance Revolution Controller
entries.subtitle: The controller moves to the floor
entries.summary: Konami's soft dance mat brought PlayStation rhythm games under your feet in 1999.
body: The PlayStation version of Dance Dance Revolution reached Japan in 1999 with a soft dance mat as a dedicated accessory. Its four directional panels turned the scrolling arrows on television into steps on the floor, bringing the arcade game's central idea into the living room.

The mat connected to the console's controller port and included controls such as Start and Select. Timing became a movement of the whole body rather than a press of the thumb. Different compatible mats and regional designs followed; the home accessory was distinct from the arcade machine's rigid metal platform.
